Auth Do you need to be logged in? (or is it open to anyone?)
DB Does it read or write the database? Which tables?
External Does it call the outside world? (Stripe, a webhook, an API…)
Async Does it kick off a background job? (Celery, a thread…)
Cache Does it read or invalidate the cache? Which keys?
PII Does it touch personal data (email, phone, address…)?

Severity colors — Lenscheck ranks every finding by how much it should worry you:

  • 🔴 critical — security / data-flow (e.g. an open endpoint writing to the DB)
  • 🟠 high — money paths (payments, orders)
  • 🟡 medium — a new write or a dependency change
  • 🟢 low — a safe refactor, nothing risky

PII — "Personally Identifiable Information": personal data like an email, phone number,
address, password, card number. Leaking it is a legal and trust problem.

PII egress — "egress" just means leaving. PII egress = personal data leaving your
server — sent to an external API, written to a log, or returned to the browser. That's the moment
that matters.

Taint — following a piece of data as it moves through the code. If an email is "tainted," Lenscheck
watches whether that exact value reaches an exit (an external call, a log, a response). If it
does, that's a confirmed leak.

Invariant — a rule your codebase has always followed, whether or not anyone wrote it down.
Example: "every endpoint that writes to the database first checks you're logged in." Lenscheck can
discover these from your git history, let you confirm the real ones, and then enforce
them on every PR.

Semantic diff — a normal diff compares text. A semantic diff compares meaning: Lenscheck
analyzes your code before and after the PR and reports the difference in behavior (new
endpoints, new DB writes, new calls…), ignoring cosmetic changes like renaming a function.

📌Companion tool: lenscheck-contract

Everything above happens before merge — the reviewer discovers the rules your code follows and
flags a PR that breaks one. Its companion, lenscheck-contract
(a tiny, MIT-licensed runtime library), closes the loop at runtime: your app keeps a declared list
of what each endpoint is allowed to do — write these tables, call these hosts — and can't lie about
it. An undeclared DB write or a new external call is blocked (or logged) the moment it happens.

So a rule you confirmed here — "auth before any DB write," "personal data never leaves without
auth" — can be declared once and enforced in production, not just checked in review. Same
promise, two moments: the reviewer catches it in the PR; the contract stops it in prod. →
Read the contract guide.

Lenscheck is source-available (Elastic-2.0). Built by Ankush Singh Gandhi. Questions,
stars, and sponsorships welcome on GitHub.

articles.title: We measured what AI coding agents preload into their prompts. It wastes 99.6% of context and misses the runtime entity 53% of the time.
articles.description: Published by Lucen Research Group · November 2026 · Peer-Verified Empirical Report   An AI agent was...
articles.body_html:
Published by Lucen Research Group · November 2026 · Peer-Verified Empirical Report

An AI agent was tasked with triaging a production database connection exhaustion incident. To give it the tools it needed, the host platform preloaded all 50 Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers into its system prompt. That was 272,607 tokens of raw JSON schemas.

Two tools would have solved the incident: pg_check_connection_pool and slack_post_incident_bulletin. The agent preloaded five hundred.

The model choked on prompt prefill, confused two similarly-named PostgreSQL diagnostics tools, and halted because it had zero pre-bound connection credentials.

Not a crash. Not an error. The context dump was provably complete with respect to the MCP manifests. Every tool the enterprise owned was in the prompt. The entity that mattered — the target primary cluster endpoint (pg-cluster-prod.internal:5432) — was simply never bound, and dumping more schemas into the context window could never produce an entity that was never resolved.

That one case sent us down a hole for a week. Here is what came out of it: across 50 realistic enterprise operational scenarios in multi-server environments, the naive context dumps coding agents rely on consume 272,607 tokens per query with a 0% Turn-0 success rate. Carefully tuned keyword and BM25 retrievers: 46.7%. And no amount of prompt tuning fixes an edge the system never extracted.

So we built the thing that acts on that number: Lucen, a deterministic context resolution layer built directly on HydraDB and SlateDB. And we made every figure in this article re-derivable with one command, because empirical systems only deserve trust when a reader can knock the numbers down and fail.

FIGURE 1: THE RESOLUTION GAP (272,607 TOKENS VS 1,214 TOKENS)


Live view of the 4-tier context resolution graph inside HydraDB: MCP Servers (Blue), Capabilities (Yellow), Isolated Tools (Red), and Bound Entities (Emerald) resolved in 0.21 ms.

1. The Problem Nobody Measured

Every agent framework works from a context mechanism. In small demos, developers serialize every available tool into the system prompt. It is fast, intuitive, and feels complete.

Here is the trap, stated as a pair:

  • What naive prompt preloading guarantees: The context is complete with respect to every tool schema the servers declare.
  • What the agent actually needs: The context contains only the tools reachable for the task, pre-bound with active runtime infrastructure entities.

Those are fundamentally different properties, and the gap between them is invisible from inside the tool. A prompt can be perfectly formed and still be missing runtime infrastructure roads. An agent that hallucinates a parameter or requires 3 exploratory turns looks like an LLM limitation, when it is really a context retrieval failure.

So the question was never "can LLMs read 200k tokens?" It was the cheaper question nobody asked: is dumping the entire catalog into the context window any good?

FIGURE 2: 4-LAYER SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE (HYDRADB + SLATEDB + S3)


Client Layer (MCP Gateway), Context Broker (FastAPI), GraphBLAS Traversal Kernel (SciPy/CSR), and Storage Backend (HydraDB + SlateDB on MinIO S3).

2. How We Measured It

To ground the benchmark in enterprise reality rather than synthetic toy prompts, we curated a 50-task operational corpus partitioned into:

  • 35 Training Tasks: Used for initial topology calibration and continual feedback weight reinforcement.
  • 15 Strictly Held-Out Test Tasks: Completely unseen composite operational incidents spanning database pool exhaustion, container OOM rolling restarts, CloudWatch IOPS degradation, hotfix PR review, and multi-region failover.

We evaluated 5 competing arms across the catalog of 500 MCP tools and 80 runtime entities:

  1. Naive Full Preload: Dumps all 500 tool schemas (272,607 tokens) into the prompt.
  2. Standard BM25 Top-4: Keyword retrieval ranking tool names and descriptions.
  3. Hardened BM25 (k=8 + Query Decomposition + Flat Dict): Splits compound queries into sub-clauses and resolves entities via a static {tool: entity} map.
  4. Hardened BM25 (k=16 + Learned Boost): Multiplies scores by empirical feedback weights at k=16 (7,653 tokens).
  5. Lucen (HydraDB GraphBLAS): Executes multi-hop topological reachability and pre-binds entities in a single atomic Cypher query.

TABLE 1: 5-ARM HELD-OUT EMPIRICAL RESULTS (15 UNSEEN TASKS)

Arm Tool Recall Entity Recall Turn-0 Execution Avg Tokens Latency
1. Naive Preload 100.0% 0.0% 0.0% (0/15) 272,607 0.0 ms
2a. BM25 Top-4 70.0% 0.0% 0.0% (0/15) 2,273 0.85 ms
2b. Hardened BM25 (k=8 + Dict) 66.7% 100.0% 46.7% (7/15) 4,229 1.42 ms
2c. Hardened BM25 (k=16 + Boost) 80.0% 100.0% 66.7% (10/15) 7,653 2.15 ms
3. Lucen (HydraDB GraphBLAS) 93.3% 100.0% 86.7% (13/15) 2,211 (-99.2%) 0.21 ms (CSR)

3. Why Flat Stores & Vector Maps Miss

We expected the baseline failures to be basic vocabulary mismatches. They mostly were not.

Even when we gave the vector baseline an unfair advantage — a static {tool_id: bound_entity} key-value dictionary and expanded retrieval to $k=16$ with query decomposition — its Turn-0 task success stalled at 66.7% while burning 7,653 tokens.

The trap is contextual multi-instance disambiguation:

In enterprise operations, a tool like pg_check_connection_pool attaches to multiple database clusters: pg-cluster-prod, pg-cluster-staging, and pg-cluster-analytics. A static dictionary always returns the same hardcoded instance. If an incident strikes staging or a regional replica, a flat store binds the wrong cluster and the agent executes actions against the wrong database.

HydraDB resolves this because it stores structural reachability:

(:Service {env: 'prod'})-[:RUNS_IN]->(:Environment)-[:USES_DB]->(:DatabaseCluster)

The correct entity is resolved not by string matching, but by traversing graph reachability from the calling agent's operational scope.

FIGURE 3: THE STEP-BY-STEP RESOLUTION PIPELINE

4. Why It Lives Inside HydraDB

HydraDB is the measuring instrument and the routing kernel here, not a passive storage dump. Four core properties run inside the engine:

1. Embedded SlateDB on MinIO/S3

Unlike volatile in-memory Python dictionaries that vanish when an agent container restarts, HydraDB writes immutable SSTables and write-ahead logs directly to S3-compatible object storage via SlateDB (http://localhost:9000/hydra-graph-store). State is durable, decoupled, and persistent.

2. SuiteSparse GraphBLAS CSR Formulation

HydraDB compiles relationship edges into compressed sparse adjacency matrices. Given a one-hot capability vector x, candidate tools are resolved via matrix semiring multiplication:

y = x @ (A_provides * W_prefers)

Executing in 0.21 ms locally, ensuring traversal speed is independent of graph density.

3. Declarative OpenCypher Pattern Matching

Tool pruning, preference weighting, and entity pre-binding execute as a single OpenCypher query:

MATCH (c:Capability) WHERE c.id IN ["cap_db_diagnostics", "cap_incident_alerting"]
MATCH (t:Tool)-[:PROVIDES]->(c)
OPTIONAL MATCH (c)-[p:PREFERS]->(t)
WITH t, c, coalesce(p.weight, 1.0) AS relevance_weight
OPTIONAL MATCH (t)-[r:REQUIRES_ENTITY|RESOLVES_ENTITY]->(e:Entity)
RETURN t, c, e, relevance_weight
ORDER BY relevance_weight DESC LIMIT 2;

4. In-Engine Dynamic Edge Reweighting

When an agent successfully completes an action, HydraDB updates the graph using atomic Cypher writes:
MERGE (c)-[p:PREFERS]->(t) SET p.weight = p.weight + 0.15.
Unlike SQLite, which serializes writes under a single database lock causing p99 tail spikes (2.48 ms), HydraDB updates point edges cleanly without relational table contention.

TABLE 2: EMPIRICAL ABLATION (FLAT STORE VS HYDRADB)

Storage Engine 1-Hop 3-Hop Path Concurrent p99 Durability & Architecture Finding
Python Dict (In-Memory) 0.000 ms 0.001 ms 0.005 ms Volatile heap: state vanishes on restart
SQLite (Tuned WAL) 0.009 ms 0.016 ms 2.480 ms Single-file lock: write serialization spike
Lucen Embedded (Local CSR) 0.212 ms 0.285 ms 285.2 ms Fast in-process topological routing
HydraDB Cluster over HTTP 6.420 ms 7.150 ms 8.920 ms SlateDB LSM SSTs, multi-agent S3 durability

5. The Drop-In MCP Gateway

A context layer that requires rewriting agent code will never be adopted. So Lucen ships as a standard Model Context Protocol (MCP) stdio gateway:

In claude_desktop_config.json or .cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "lucen": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "backend.mcp_gateway"]
    }
  }
}

The gateway exposes lucen_find_tools and lucen_record_feedback alongside runnable tool handlers (pg_check_connection_pool, slack_post_incident_bulletin).

Agents query the gateway; Lucen traverses HydraDB in sub-millisecond time, mounts only reachable schemas, and injects runtime endpoints into the turn. Secrets (API keys, private tokens) remain isolated inside the gateway, preventing credential leakage into model prompts.

6. What We'd Push Back on Ourselves

Because measurement articles get the scrutiny they deserve:

  • 50 Scenarios is not 10,000: While our 50-task corpus covers diverse infrastructure failures, larger multi-tenant enterprise topologies will expose edge cases in capability mapping.
  • Network Latency Disclosure: In-process SciPy CSR executes in 0.21 ms, while HydraDB cluster roundtrips over HTTP take 6.42 ms. We report both transparently.
  • The Causal Negative Control: To prove that graph topology is strictly load-bearing rather than accidental heuristics, we randomly ablated edges from the graph. Task success collapsed from 86.7% to 0.0%.

FIGURE 4: CAUSAL NEGATIVE CONTROL (EDGE ABLATION)

7. Check It Yourself (Reproduce Locally)

Every figure in this article is emitted by committed scripts and re-derivable with one command:

# Asserts 6/6 engine checks
$ python lucen.py verify

# Re-runs 5-arm evaluation across seeds
$ python eval/benchmark_eval.py

# Re-runs Dict vs SQLite vs HydraDB ablation
$ python eval/ablation_flat_store.py

8. The Engineering Journey: 4 Technical Challenges We Faced & How HydraDB Solved Them

When we started building Lucen for Hack Hydra 2026, our thesis was simple: LLM agents do not need larger context windows; they need topologically constrained working memory. But bridging high-throughput autonomous agent loops with a persistent graph store surfaced four severe engineering bottlenecks. Here is how HydraDB enabled us to solve each one.

Challenge 01: The 272k-Token Preload Wall & The Parameter Void

  • The Bottleneck: In multi-server enterprise setups, loading 50 Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers serializes 500 tool definitions into the prompt (272,607 tokens). Standard vector similarity search finds tool names based on query embeddings, but leaves required parameter schemas unpopulated. The agent is forced to hallucinate production endpoints or waste multi-turn dialogs discovering infrastructure parameters.
  • How HydraDB Solved It: HydraDB models the relationship between capabilities, tools, and infrastructure entities as a typed property graph. Using declarative OpenCypher, Lucen executes a single multi-hop query: 
MATCH (c:Capability) WHERE c.id IN $matched_caps
MATCH (t:Tool)-[:PROVIDES]->(c)
MATCH (t)-[:REQUIRES_ENTITY]->(e:Entity)
RETURN t, e;
  • Result: Prunes 498 unneeded tools in 1.8ms and directly injects active credentials (e.g., pg-cluster-prod.internal:5432), eliminating parameter hallucination and driving context reduction by 99.6%.

Challenge 02: Sub-Millisecond Latency vs Object Store Durability

  • The Bottleneck: Autonomous agents make rapid sequential decisions. Adding a 500ms remote database network hop on every turn degrades execution speed. Conversely, storing graph adjacency in Python heap memory means all organizational routing history is lost when agent pods recycle.
  • How HydraDB Solved It: HydraDB's core architecture decouples in-memory sparse matrix execution from durable cloud storage. We compile the topology into compressed sparse row (CSR) matrices using SuiteSparse GraphBLAS primitives for instantaneous in-process evaluation (0.21 ms). Concurrently, HydraDB writes write-ahead logs and SSTables directly to S3-compatible object storage via SlateDB, delivering true zero-loss durability across container lifecycles.

Challenge 03: Multi-Agent Concurrent Learning Without Lock Spikes

  • The Bottleneck: We wanted the graph to learn continuously: successful tool executions reinforce preference edges, while failures apply penalties. In our empirical ablation tests, SQLite suffered severe lock contention under 100 concurrent agent writers, causing p99 latency to spike to 2.48 ms due to database-level write serialization.
  • How HydraDB Solved It: HydraDB performs atomic point-in-time Cypher updates: 
MERGE (c:Capability {id: $cap_id})-[p:PREFERS]->(t:Tool {id: $tool_id})
SET p.weight = p.weight + 0.15;
  • Result: Dynamic Thompson sampling edge updates execute concurrently with zero lost updates and zero relational table locking.

Challenge 04: Runtime Tool Crashes & Autonomous Recovery

  • The Bottleneck: When an agent's primary diagnostic tool encounters a connection timeout or 504 gateway error in production, standard systems abort or loop infinitely re-prompting the user.
  • How HydraDB Solved It: We indexed recovery fallbacks directly into HydraDB as :FALLBACK_TO relationships. When pg_check_connection_pool fails, the engine executes pattern-matching failover in 0.04 ms, immediately routing to postgres_stream_logs and pre-binding the healthy read replica (pg-cluster-prod-ro-01.internal:5432) with zero agent re-querying.

Links & Verification

  • Live Interactive Demo: https://lucen-app.onrender.com
  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/toufiqfarhan0/hydradb-hack-nov
  • Live Traversal Console: https://lucen-app.onrender.com/console
  • Complete Docs: https://lucen-app.onrender.com/docs

articles.title: Uploading straight from the browser to DigitalOcean Spaces
articles.description: Spaces Gallery is a small Flask app I maintain that uploads images to DigitalOcean Spaces and shows...
articles.body_html:
Spaces Gallery is a small Flask app I maintain that uploads images to DigitalOcean Spaces and shows them in a gallery. Right now every upload goes through the app. The browser sends the file to Flask, Flask checks it, makes a thumbnail and writes both to Spaces.

The usual advice is to skip that middle step. The app hands the browser a presigned POST, a short-lived signed form, and the browser sends the file straight to Spaces. I built that into the gallery and measured what it changes, using the app's own code and deployment setup.

The setup

The app ran under gunicorn exactly as its Procfile starts it, which means one sync worker, on a 1 GB Droplet in Frankfurt. The Spaces bucket was in Frankfurt too. My laptop played the browser, uploading noise PNGs of 1, 4 and 8 MB that can't be compressed. On the Droplet, a sampler recorded the app's CPU time, memory and network traffic four times a second.

The direct path has three steps:

  1. The page asks the app for a presigned POST. The policy pins the object key, the content type and the ACL, and caps the size at 8 MB.
  2. The browser posts the file to Spaces.
  3. The page tells the app it's done. The app downloads the file, checks that it really is an image, makes the thumbnail and sets the cache header.

That last step exists because a policy can limit a file's size and declared type, but it can't look inside it.

Spaces enforces the policy

Before any timing, I checked that Spaces actually holds the line:

  • A file sent with Content-Type: text/html against a policy that says image/png got a 403.
  • A 9 MB file against the 8 MB limit got a 400.
  • A five-byte file called fake.png was accepted, since the policy can't tell. The app's check then found it wasn't an image and deleted it.

So the size and type limits move from the app to Spaces, and the "is this really an image" check stays in the app.

Cache-Control is checked and then thrown away

The gallery gives every upload Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, so the CDN and browsers keep images for a year. I put that header in the presigned policy like the others. The upload worked, and the stored object had no Cache-Control at all.

Spaces does read the condition. Leaving the field out or sending a different value got a 403. But with the right value, the object was stored without the header. The lowercase field name behaved the same. The thumbnail, written by the app through the normal API, had the header as expected.

The fix is a copy of the object onto itself, with the metadata replaced, in the finish step. That's one request, and no file data passes through the app for it. After it, the public URL returned the one-year cache header.

For one upload, it wasn't faster

I expected the direct path to win easily. Over five runs of each size, the medians were:

File Through the app Direct Direct, sending to Spaces only
1 MB 0.73 s 1.15 s 0.08 s
4 MB 0.86 s 0.87 s 0.16 s
8 MB 1.04 s 1.05 s 0.26 s

The transfer to Spaces was quick. My connection is fast, and 8 MB took a quarter of a second. But the direct path adds two calls to the app around it. For the 8 MB file, the presign took 0.21 s and the finish step 0.57 s. Those two together cost as much as the transfer saved, and for small files they cost more.

The app still touched every byte

The sampler first said that the proxied upload received 8 MB and sent almost nothing to Spaces. That couldn't be right. The traffic to Spaces in the same region was going over the Droplet's second network interface, eth1, which I hadn't been counting. With both interfaces counted, an 8 MB upload looked like this:

  • Through the app: 8.3 MB in from the client and 8.4 MB out to Spaces, the file plus its thumbnail.
  • Direct: nothing from the client, but 8.0 MB in from Spaces during the finish step, which downloads the file to check it, and 0.4 MB out for the thumbnail.

CPU time was about the same either way, 0.53 to 0.6 seconds per upload, almost all of it Pillow decoding the image and making the thumbnail. The direct path moved the upload off the app, but the finish step brings the file straight back.

Ten at once

With ten 8 MB uploads started together at full speed, the single worker handled them one at a time either way. Through the app, they finished about 0.9 seconds apart, the last after 9.0 seconds. A health check sent during the batch waited 8.8 seconds for an answer.

Direct, all ten finished in 7.6 seconds and the health check waited up to 4.3. Better, because the transfers themselves ran in parallel, but the finish steps still queued behind each other on the one worker.

Slow clients are where it matters

A laptop on a fast connection is the best case for proxying. So I throttled three clients to 1 MB per second and had each upload 8 MB, while a health check ran every half second.

Every upload took between 8.6 and 10.4 seconds either way, since the connection set the pace. The difference was everyone else. Through the app, one health check took 10.1 seconds, the whole length of the batch. The worker was busy reading slow request bodies and nothing else got in. Direct, the slowest of 25 health checks took 0.87 seconds. The app only saw the quick presign and finish calls, and the slow part happened between the browser and Spaces.

That's the real argument for direct uploads with a single small worker. They don't make one upload faster, they stop slow uploads from freezing the app.

Without CORS, uploads fail and succeed at the same time

A browser will only let the page post to Spaces if the bucket allows the app's origin. I tried it first without a CORS rule. The page's fetch threw "Failed to fetch", so it showed an error and never called the finish step.

The file was in the bucket anyway. A plain form POST doesn't need the browser to ask permission first. It sends the request and then refuses to let the page read the response. So Spaces stored the upload, and the page believed it had failed. Two test images ended up in the gallery with no thumbnail, no cache header and no image check.

Adding a CORS rule for the app's origin, allowing POST, fixed the browser side. I also changed the page so that a network error still goes on to the finish step, which either finds the file and completes it or reports it missing. With the rule removed again, an upload from Chrome then finished normally, thumbnail and all.

What I got wrong

I expected the direct path to be faster per upload. On a fast connection it wasn't, and for a 1 MB file it was slower, because two extra calls to the app cost more than the transfer.

My first traffic numbers were wrong, because the sampler only counted eth0. They made it look as though the proxied upload never reached Spaces.

I assumed a Cache-Control field in the policy would set the header, since Spaces checks it. It doesn't, and I'd have shipped uploads without their year-long cache header if I hadn't looked at the stored object.

And I took "Failed to fetch" to mean the upload had failed. It meant the browser wouldn't show the page the answer.

Caveats

This is one Droplet size, with the single worker the Procfile gives, and one region, with my laptop as the client. The slow clients were throttled in software. The single-upload timings are five runs each, and the concurrent and slow tests ran once. I ran the app on a Droplet so I could watch its processes. On App Platform, the load balancer in front of the app might buffer request bodies, which would change the slow-client result, and I didn't test that. The bucket and the Droplet existed for about 15 minutes, which cost well under a cent.

What I'd take from it

  • Use presigned POSTs to protect the app from slow uploads, not to make uploads faster. On a fast connection they were no quicker.
  • Put the size and type limits in the policy, because Spaces enforces them, and keep a server-side check for what a policy can't see.
  • Don't rely on the policy for Cache-Control. Set it afterwards with a copy onto the same key.
  • Add the CORS rule before switching the page over, and treat a network error from the upload as "unknown", not "failed".
  • If the server still downloads every file to check it, the bytes come back anyway. The thumbnail step is the next thing to move.

articles.title: BUILDING KYNTHERA: TURNING AI AGENT FAILURES INTO RECOVERY INTELLIGENCE WITH HYDRADB
articles.description: Building Kynthera: Turning AI Agent Failures into Recovery Intelligence with HydraDB   How I...
articles.body_html:
Building Kynthera: Turning AI Agent Failures into Recovery Intelligence with HydraDB

How I built a graph-powered recovery workspace, worked through GraphBLAS and Rust deployment challenges, and connected an open-source HydraDB instance to a live application.

By Jayeoba Tunmise Paul (Jayking)

Built for the HydraDB Hackathon | Track 1: The Self-Improving Graph

1. The Problem That Made Me Build Kynthera

One thing I've noticed while building software and working with AI-powered systems is how often we solve the same problems more than once.

A dependency upgrade breaks a build. An API request starts failing. A service crashes unexpectedly. An authentication configuration stops working.

We investigate the issue, read through logs, experiment with possible fixes, and eventually find something that works.

Then we move on.

The problem is that the knowledge gained during that investigation often stays in a terminal session, a temporary conversation, or someone's memory.

When a similar failure happens again, another developer or AI agent may have to repeat much of the investigation.

That got me thinking:

What if software systems could remember their failures, understand which recovery strategies worked, and use that knowledge to make better recommendations next time?

That question became Kynthera.

Kynthera is a recovery intelligence workspace designed to turn incidents, recovery strategies, and recorded outcomes into reusable operational knowledge.

The idea is simple:

Failure is data. Recovery is intelligence.

Instead of treating an incident as something to fix and forget, Kynthera treats it as an opportunity to improve future recovery decisions.

2. Introducing Kynthera

Kynthera is a web application built around a recovery knowledge graph.

It gives developers and teams a place to record failures, create recovery strategies, connect strategies to incidents, and record whether an attempted recovery succeeded.

Over time, those records can be used to recommend relevant recovery strategies when similar incidents occur.

The application includes:

  • Incident capture: Record the failure title, signature, environment, affected service, severity, and description.
  • Recovery strategy library: Save possible recovery approaches and the failure patterns they address.
  • Recovery recommendations: Rank existing strategies against an incident using similarity, environment, and historical outcomes.
  • Feedback recording: Track whether a recovery strategy succeeded or failed.
  • Knowledge graph: Represent connections between incidents and the strategies used to recover from them.
  • Replay lab: Re-evaluate recorded incidents against the current strategy-ranking logic.
  • Recovery dashboard: Explore incidents, strategies, and accumulated recovery evidence.

The goal isn't to automate every possible fix immediately.

It's to build a reliable foundation where recovery knowledge can be captured, connected, evaluated, and reused.

Live application: https://kynthera.vercel.app

GitHub: https://github.com/paulos-ui/Kynthera

Demo walkthrough: https://www.loom.com/share/78cb0770200c4e6f808d8d8764f489b2

3. Why I Chose HydraDB

When I started designing Kynthera, I considered how recovery information should be stored.

A traditional database can store incidents and strategies in separate tables, with relationships represented through identifiers.

That approach works, but the central idea behind Kynthera is about connections.

An incident may resemble several previous incidents.

Multiple incidents may point toward the same recovery strategy.

A strategy may succeed in one environment but fail in another.

As more outcomes are recorded, the useful part of the data becomes the relationships between these records.

That's where HydraDB became interesting to me.

I wanted to explore how an open-source graph database could support a product that learns from recorded recovery history.

In Kynthera, HydraDB provides the graph storage layer for incidents, strategies, and events.

The application creates graph records and connects incidents to recovery strategies through relationships such as:

(i)-[:RECOVERED_WITH]->(r)

Here:

  • i represents an incident.
  • r represents a recovery strategy.
  • RECOVERED_WITH records the relationship between them.

This is useful because recovery knowledge is not just a collection of independent documents.

It's a network of experiences and outcomes.

For the initial implementation, I use HydraDB primarily as the graph-backed persistence and relationship layer. The recommendation scoring itself currently runs in the application.

That separation is important: HydraDB stores the connected knowledge, while Kynthera's ranking engine determines how existing recovery evidence should influence suggestions.

4. How Kynthera Works

The recovery workflow follows a straightforward cycle.

Step 1: Capture an incident

A developer opens the Kynthera console and records a failure.

For example:

Incident: Build fails after dependency upgrade

Failure signature: npm ERESOLVE react peer dependency

Environment: Node.js

Service: Frontend application

Severity: Medium

Description: An application fails to install dependencies after upgrading a package because of incompatible peer dependency requirements.

The incident becomes a record Kynthera can reference later.

Step 2: Create recovery strategies

A developer can create strategies for resolving similar failures.

For example, a strategy might involve reviewing conflicting dependency versions, checking compatibility requirements, and selecting a compatible package combination.

Rather than keeping that knowledge in a temporary troubleshooting conversation, Kynthera stores the strategy as a reusable record.

Step 3: Recommend relevant strategies

When an incident is reviewed, Kynthera compares it against known recovery strategies.

The current ranking logic considers three factors:

  1. Similarity between failure signatures.
  2. Whether the runtime environments match.
  3. Historical success and failure feedback.

The engine combines these signals into a recommendation score.

Step 4: Record the outcome

After trying a strategy, the user records whether it worked.

That feedback updates the strategy's success or failure counts.

The next time a related incident is evaluated, the updated history contributes to its score.

Step 5: Replay previous incidents

The replay lab evaluates previously recorded successful incidents using the current ranking logic.

This helps developers inspect whether the strategies ranked highest are consistent with recorded recovery choices.

It provides a way to examine the system's behavior as the knowledge base grows.

Importantly, this is currently a descriptive replay over recorded data, not a controlled evaluation against an independent test dataset.

5. The Technical Architecture

Kynthera uses a fairly focused stack.

Layer Technology
Frontend Next.js, React, TypeScript
Deployment Vercel
Authentication Google OAuth through NextAuth
Graph database Open-source HydraDB
Local development Ubuntu on WSL
Cloud graph hosting Render
Graph access HydraDB HTTP interface and Bolt adapter
Recovery logic Application-level ranking and feedback engine

The application is divided into three main parts.

Frontend workspace

The frontend gives users a place to capture incidents, manage recovery strategies, explore graph relationships, and review recommendations.

I wanted it to feel like a focused engineering tool rather than a generic analytics dashboard.

The interface follows a dark visual direction with bright green accents, matching the concept of an intelligence workspace.

Application backend

Next.js server routes handle the application's operations.

They read and update incident records, evaluate recovery strategies, record feedback, and communicate with the selected storage backend.

Authentication protects the workspace, and records include an owner identifier so data can be separated by account.

This is a starting isolation model, not a claim that the system has completed a production security audit.

HydraDB graph layer

HydraDB stores the connected records.

The adapter supports creating and retrieving graph entities, along with relationships linking incidents and recovery strategies.

It also preserves Kynthera's application-generated identifiers alongside the graph's native identifiers.

This keeps the application's internal record references consistent while using HydraDB as the underlying graph engine.

6. Building the Recommendation Engine

One of the most important design decisions was figuring out how the system should recommend recovery strategies.

I didn't want to start with an opaque model that generated suggestions without showing why they were selected.

Instead, I implemented a transparent ranking mechanism.

The current engine calculates a weighted score from three signals.

Failure signature similarity: 54%

The system tokenizes the incident and strategy signatures, then measures the overlap between their meaningful terms.

For example, an incident containing ERESOLVE, react, and dependency would have a stronger signature match with a strategy addressing a React dependency conflict than one addressing an unrelated database timeout.

Environment match: 20%

Recovery advice can depend heavily on the runtime.

A Node.js dependency issue and a Python package-resolution problem might look similar at a high level, but their solutions can differ.

The engine gives additional weight when the incident and strategy share the same environment.

Historical outcome quality: 26%

The engine also considers recorded successes and failures.

Its current outcome-quality calculation uses:

(successes + 1) / (successes + failures + 2)

This avoids giving an untested strategy an extreme score simply because it has no recorded failures.

The overall score is calculated as:

Score = 100 × (
  0.54 × signature_similarity
  + 0.20 × environment_match
  + 0.26 × outcome_quality
)

The resulting strategies are ordered by score.

Kynthera also displays reasons behind the ranking, including signature similarity, runtime match, and historical feedback.

I chose this approach because it is understandable and testable.

As the product evolves, the ranking formula can be compared against other approaches using a stronger evaluation dataset.

The current weights are design choices, not empirically optimized coefficients.

7. The Hardest Part Was Getting HydraDB Running

Building the interface was only one part of this project.

The more interesting challenge was getting the open-source HydraDB engine working in my development environment and connecting it to the application.

I was developing on Windows using Ubuntu through WSL.

At first, I expected to install the required dependencies, build the database engine, start a node, and connect the application.

In practice, several problems appeared along the way.

Challenge 1: Missing LAGraph dependencies

One of the early problems involved LAGraph, a graph algorithms library associated with the GraphBLAS ecosystem.

The build process needed compatible dependencies to be available in the expected locations.

When they weren't, the build couldn't complete cleanly.

I had to investigate the dependency requirements and how the relevant native libraries were being discovered during compilation.

The lesson here was that a Rust-based project can still depend on a substantial native C/C++ ecosystem.

Getting the Rust toolchain installed is not always enough.

Challenge 2: GraphBLAS configuration

GraphBLAS was another important part of the setup.

I encountered configuration and library-discovery issues while preparing the build environment.

This required checking dependency paths and making sure the native libraries and headers were available to the build process.

The underlying problem wasn't related to Kynthera's UI or business logic.

It came from the database engine's native build dependencies.

This was a useful reminder that infrastructure work often involves understanding multiple layers of a software stack.

Challenge 3: Rust linker failures

Once I got further into the build process, I ran into Rust linking problems.

The compiler could progress through parts of the project, but linking the final executable depended on native libraries being properly configured.

I worked through the errors, adjusted the local environment, and continued rebuilding until I could start the HydraDB graph node successfully.

That moment was an important milestone.

Instead of relying on a hypothetical database integration, I had a running open-source graph engine on my machine.

Challenge 4: Connecting the graph node to Kynthera

After starting HydraDB locally, the next problem was connectivity.

Kynthera's frontend was already deployed on Vercel, but the graph database was running inside my local WSL environment.

A cloud-hosted application cannot simply connect to a database listening on localhost inside my laptop.

I initially used a tunnel to expose the local service for testing.

I also had to work through authentication and connection configuration so the application's backend could send graph queries successfully.

This stage taught me an important distinction:

A running database is not the same thing as an application that can reliably reach and authenticate with that database.

The endpoint, credentials, request format, and deployment environment all have to agree.

8. Moving HydraDB From My Laptop to Render

After getting the local integration working, another question came up.

What happens when I turn off my laptop?

With HydraDB running inside WSL, the graph service depends on my computer being powered on and the relevant processes continuing to run.

That wasn't ideal for a publicly accessible hackathon demo.

I explored cloud hosting options, including Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud, but ultimately chose Render for a simpler initial deployment.

I deployed the HydraDB graph node using a container image and configured the service to initialize its graph storage directory.

The first deployment failed because the configured local storage directory didn't exist.

After addressing that, I encountered another failure caused by an incorrect executable path in the custom startup command.

Once those issues were corrected, the service started successfully.

The logs showed the graph-node listeners starting, and the deployed service became reachable through its Render URL.

I then tested its health endpoint:

https://kynthera-hydradb.onrender.com/healthz

The response was:

{
  "status": "ok"
}

That confirmed the service was responding to health checks.

It did not, by itself, prove that every graph operation was working, so authenticated query testing was a separate step.

Connecting Render to Vercel

I added a separate set of environment variables for the Render connection while preserving the local configuration.

That allowed Kynthera to select between the local HydraDB node and the Render-hosted instance.

The application now supports an explicit connection target rather than requiring the local configuration to be deleted whenever I want to use the hosted database.

This also makes development easier because I can keep working against a local instance when needed.

An important limitation of the free deployment

The Render deployment is useful for demonstration and development, but the free service has limitations.

It can become idle, and the temporary filesystem isn't durable storage for a graph database.

That means locally stored graph data may be lost when the service restarts or is replaced.

For production use, Kynthera still needs a persistent storage setup and a more complete operational plan.

I consider the current deployment a working infrastructure milestone, not the final production architecture.

9. What Makes the Graph Useful?

The biggest value of HydraDB in Kynthera is the ability to treat recovery knowledge as connected information.

Consider three incidents:

  • A frontend build fails after a dependency upgrade.
  • Another project encounters a similar package conflict.
  • A third service breaks because of incompatible library versions.

These incidents may share a recovery approach even if they occurred in different projects.

A graph can preserve that shared relationship.

As more incidents and strategies are recorded, Kynthera has a foundation for exploring questions such as:

  • Which recovery strategies have been associated with similar failures?
  • Which strategies have a history of successful outcomes?
  • Are certain failures recurring across services?
  • Do some strategies perform differently depending on the environment?
  • Which recorded recoveries should be investigated further?

The current implementation already connects incidents and strategies and uses stored outcome data during recommendation ranking.

More advanced graph traversal, pattern discovery, and automated agent feedback remain opportunities for future development.

This is what attracted me to the hackathon's self-improving graph track.

The objective isn't simply to store more logs.

It's to organize operational experience so that future decisions can make better use of what the system has already encountered.

10. Testing and Measuring Improvement

A self-improving system needs a way to evaluate whether it's actually improving.

I implemented a replay mechanism in Kynthera to examine recorded recovery decisions.

For incidents with successful recorded outcomes, the replay engine ranks available strategies and checks whether its top recommendation matches the strategy associated with the recorded incident.

The application reports:

  • Number of recorded examples evaluated.
  • Top-one strategy match rate.
  • Expected strategy.
  • Predicted strategy.
  • Recommendation score.

This provides an initial way to inspect ranking behavior.

However, I want to be careful about what these numbers mean.

The replay currently uses previously recorded examples, and the ranking engine can use feedback derived from those records.

Therefore, the replay result should not be described as independent predictive accuracy.

It is a descriptive evaluation of the current strategy-ranking behavior.

What's still needed?

The next step is to create a proper benchmark.

I want to compare:

Baseline: Recommendations based primarily on failure-signature similarity.

Improved approach: Recommendations that incorporate environment context and historical recovery outcomes.

To evaluate them fairly, I would need a separate test set, consistent incident examples, and a clear definition of successful recommendation.

Useful metrics would include:

  • Top-one recommendation accuracy.
  • Top-three recommendation recall.
  • Recommendation latency.
  • Recovery success rate.
  • Performance across different failure categories.

I haven't established a verified improvement percentage yet, so I don't want to invent one.

The real achievement at this stage is building the system and the evaluation foundation needed to test that hypothesis.

11. What I Learned From Building Kynthera

This project taught me several things.

Infrastructure can be harder than the interface

A polished frontend is important, but a working database connection depends on much more than UI development.

Native dependencies, runtime configuration, authentication, networking, and deployment all have to work together.

Explicit reasoning is valuable

I deliberately started with a recommendation engine that can explain why it ranks a strategy highly.

That makes debugging easier and gives developers a way to challenge or improve its decisions.

Feedback needs context

A successful recovery strategy isn't automatically the best strategy for every future incident.

Environment differences, failure signatures, and the amount of recorded evidence matter.

A green health check isn't enough

Seeing a service respond to /healthz is useful, but it isn't a substitute for testing authenticated queries, reading and writing graph records, and confirming persistence.

Self-improvement must be demonstrated

It's tempting to describe any feedback-based system as self-improving.

But genuine improvement should be backed by repeatable measurements.

Kynthera provides a starting point for that process. The next challenge is proving how much the accumulated evidence improves recovery recommendations.

12. What's Next for Kynthera?

There are several directions I want to explore.

1. Persistent graph storage

Move beyond temporary free-tier storage so recovery knowledge survives restarts and deployments.

2. Better evaluation

Build a larger set of realistic incidents and compare recommendation approaches against a controlled baseline.

3. Richer graph relationships

Explore connections between environments, services, failure categories, incidents, and recovery outcomes.

4. Agent integrations

Allow AI agents to submit structured incident reports and retrieve relevant recovery knowledge through an API.

5. Automated evidence collection

Move beyond user-reported outcomes toward recoveries validated through tests, health checks, or execution evidence.

6. Safer recovery workflows

Eventually support carefully controlled recovery execution with approvals, clear permissions, and audit records.

The long-term idea is to move from a workspace that remembers failures toward infrastructure that helps automated systems recover more intelligently.

13. Final Thoughts

I started Kynthera with a simple observation.

Developers and AI agents spend a lot of time solving problems that have already been encountered somewhere before.

The missing piece is often not the solution itself.

It's the ability to preserve the experience, connect it to related failures, and retrieve it at the right moment.

Building Kynthera with HydraDB gave me an opportunity to explore that idea through a real application.

It also pushed me outside the comfort of normal frontend development.

I had to work through native graph dependencies, Rust linking errors, service authentication, deployment configuration, and the challenges of making a locally hosted database accessible to a cloud application.

Those problems were frustrating at times, but they were also the most valuable part of the experience.

Kynthera is still an early implementation.

The recommendation engine is intentionally simple, the replay system needs stronger independent evaluation, and the hosted database requires durable storage before production use.

But the core concept is working as a foundation: capture incidents, connect them to recovery strategies, record outcomes, and use that history to inform future recommendations.

That's what I wanted to build for the HydraDB Hackathon.

Failure is data. Recovery is intelligence.

And I believe AI systems should get better at recovering from failures they've already encountered.

Explore Kynthera

Live application: https://kynthera.vercel.app

GitHub repository: https://github.com/paulos-ui/Kynthera

Demo walkthrough: https://www.loom.com/share/78cb0770200c4e6f808d8d8764f489b2

Original X submission: https://x.com/__Official__1/status/2122293924488208853

Built by Jayeoba Tunmise Paul (Jayking) for the HydraDB Hackathon, using the open-source HydraDB graph engine.

Thanks for reading.

articles.title: I built an AI whiteboard that draws on the board instead of answering in chat
articles.description: One sentence in, an AWS architecture out: real cloud icons, attached connectors and a plain JSON file. With the full trace of one run.
articles.body_html:
Ask a chatbot for an architecture diagram and you get a block of Mermaid. You paste it somewhere else, the layout is off, the icons are grey boxes, and the thing that made the drawing is not the thing you fix it in.

I wanted the model to work on the same canvas I do, with the same tools I have, so that what it makes is ordinary shapes I can drag around afterwards. That became Whiboard: an online whiteboard for diagrams and plans, with an assistant that draws on the board.

There is a try page that opens a real board with no account. This post is one run on that page from start to finish: the prompt, every step the assistant took (including the one that failed), and the files that came out.

One sentence in

Draw the architecture of a web app on AWS: CloudFront in front, a load balancer, two app servers, Postgres on RDS, Redis for sessions and S3 for uploads.

It took 1 minute 22 seconds, and I did not touch the result. Here is the same board in the app:

I asked for the six services. It added the users, a VPC, an Auto Scaling group around the two servers and labels like "HTTPS" and "uploads" on its own. You may or may not want those, and it hardly matters, because none of this is a picture:

  • Every icon is a tile from the built-in library: AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Cloudflare, plus brand, dev and Linux logos. Double-click a tile to swap it.
  • Every arrow is a connector attached to the shapes at both ends. Drag App Server 2 somewhere else and its arrows follow.
  • Everything the assistant does is an undo step. ⌘Z walks its work back piece by piece.

What it did in those 82 seconds

The panel lists each step while it works. This is the whole run, copied from it:

✓ Reading the board
✓ Searching icons for "cloudfront"
✓ Searching icons for "elastic load balancing"
✓ Searching icons for "ec2"
✓ Searching icons for "rds"
✓ Searching icons for "elasticache"
✓ Searching icons for "s3"
✓ Searching icons for "user"
✓ Searching icons for "simple storage service"
  Reasoning
✓ Drawing 8 nodes, 10 connections
✓ Looking at the board
  Reasoning
✓ Searching the board for "connector"
✓ Reading the board
  Reasoning
✓ Deleting 3 elements
✗ Drawing 0 nodes, 1 connections
  Nothing to draw: give at least one node, container or label.
✓ Reading the board
✓ Searching icons for "aws cloud"
✓ Adding 1 elements
✓ Changing 1 elements
✓ Looking at the board
  Reasoning
✓ Changing 2 elements
✓ Looking at the board

Answered in 1m 22s · first output after 1.7s · 11 steps

Three things in there are worth pointing at.

It finds real icons first. Before drawing anything it searches the icon library eight times, which is why the diagram has the actual CloudFront and RDS tiles and not rectangles with names in them.

It looks at its own work. "Looking at the board" renders the board to an image and hands it back to the model. After the first draft it looked, deleted three elements and went back in to fix them.

One step failed. The line marked ✗ is the drawing tool refusing a call that had a connection and no nodes. The model read the board again and got there another way. I left it in because that is what a real run looks like.

What else you can ask it

  • Change what is already there: "make every sticky about pricing orange and put them in one column", "turn these notes into a flowchart".
  • Read a file sitting on the board. Drop a spreadsheet, a CSV, a document or a deck on the canvas and ask "how many rows are in that CSV?" or "sum up the proposal".
  • Take an image or a video as input. A video is cut into at most ten still frames in your browser; the video itself is never uploaded.

Next to the assistant are three one-click tools: Summary (key points, decisions, action items, open questions), Organize (sorts a wall of sticky notes into themes) and Ideas.

The file is yours

The other thing I wanted from a whiteboard was to be able to leave it.

There are five export formats, and all five are on every plan, the free one included: PNG, SVG, PDF, draw.io and JSON. draw.io works both ways: drop a .drawio file on a board and it becomes editable shapes and connectors, then export it back when you are done. There is also an importer for Miro boards, through Miro's API.

The JSON is the whole board, never encrypted, in a documented shape. This is from the file the board above exported, cut down to two of its 58 elements:

{
  "app": "whiboard",
  "version": 1,
  "name": "My first board",
  "exportedAt": "2026-11-16T21:40:17.313Z",
  "elements": [
    {
      "id": "uUKJoRJgdRs8AkPi",
      "boardId": "try",
      "parentId": "ZKz_bMtgIxHS4zAc",
      "x": 162,
      "y": 137,
      "w": 76,
      "h": 76,
      "rotation": 0,
      "z": "aX",
      "style": {},
      "locked": false,
      "v": { "clock": 50, "actor": "try" },
      "type": "logo",
      "props": { "icon": "aws:AmazonCloudFront", "label": "CloudFront", "hideLabel": true }
    },
    {
      "id": "1JGJUcFwig1wBTPg",
      "boardId": "try",
      "parentId": null,
      "x": 0,
      "y": 0,
      "w": 0,
      "h": 0,
      "rotation": 0,
      "z": "a7",
      "style": {
        "stroke": "#4b5563",
        "strokeWidth": 1.5,
        "fontSize": 12,
        "fontFamily": "ui-monospace, Menlo, monospace",
        "color": "#4b5563"
      },
      "locked": false,
      "v": { "clock": 24, "actor": "try" },
      "type": "connector",
      "props": {
        "start": { "elId": "VKRUptdCE37irVRL", "anchor": "r" },
        "end": { "elId": "uUKJoRJgdRs8AkPi", "anchor": "l" },
        "route": "straight",
        "startArrow": "none",
        "endArrow": "arrow",
        "label": "HTTPS",
        "labelPos": "above"
      }
    }
  ]
}

It is a flat list. A connector names the ids of the two items it joins, here the Users tile and CloudFront. You can diff the file in Git, and the import accepts the same shape, so a script can write a board and you drop the file on the canvas.

Some things do not travel yet, and I would rather say so here than have you find out:

  • Uploaded images and videos are not inside the board JSON. Items point at them by id.
  • A .drawio export has no place for freehand strokes or images, and logo tiles arrive as labelled boxes without the icon. Use JSON or SVG to keep those.

The full list is on the no lock-in page.

If you would rather script it

An API. Everything the web app does goes through one HTTP API, with an OpenAPI 3.1 document at /api/v1/openapi.json and an interactive reference.

curl -s https://whiboard.com/api/v1/boards/$BOARD_ID/snapshot \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN"

Two caveats: there are no personal access tokens yet, so you sign in as a user like the app does, and the API is not versioned for third parties yet. The API guide has the details.

An iframe. An embed puts a whole board, one frame or an area of a board on another site, view only, and visitors need no account. Reloading the page shows the board as it is now, so the architecture diagram in your docs stops going stale.

<iframe src="https://embed.whiboard.com/embed/…" title="Architecture" width="100%" height="480"
  style="border:0;border-radius:12px" loading="lazy" allowfullscreen></iframe>

SVG in, shape out. Paste SVG markup on a board and its outline becomes a shape you can fill, resize, label and connect like any other.

How it is built, briefly

  • Browser: React 19 around a Canvas 2D engine written for this, with a spatial index and level-of-detail rendering. It holds 60 fps at 5,000 items, measured on a laptop.
  • Server: a Go API, a WebSocket hub with one room per board, Redis for pub/sub and presence, MongoDB for boards, ops and versions, and an S3 bucket for files.
  • Sync: every edit is an op. If two people change the same item, the later change wins. Lose the connection and you keep editing; the changes are sent when you are back.
  • Assistant: a Claude model with tools that act on the board: read it, search the icons, draw, change, delete, look at a render. The tools run in your browser against the live canvas, which is why each call is one undo step. The trace above is those tool calls.

What it costs

Free: unlimited boards, 5 editors, 3 AI prompts a day, no card. Team is $5 per editor a month. Viewers never pay.

What it is not

  • It is only a whiteboard. There are no docs, tasks or chat in it.
  • There is no mobile app.
  • There is no voting and no timer.
  • Two people cannot type in the same note at once. The later change wins.

Try it

whiboard.com/try opens a real board in your browser with nothing to sign up for. The assistant gives you 2 prompts per IP address there, so make them count. A free account gets 3 a day, and if you sign up from that page, the board you drew moves into your account.

I would like to know what it gets wrong. Give it the architecture you actually run and tell me in the comments where the diagram falls apart.

articles.title: TypeScript `protected` vs `private` in 2026: The Inheritance Visibility Rules That Bite Teams Mid-Refactor
articles.description: TypeScript's protected and private modifiers look similar but enforce wildly different visibility rules during inheritance. Teams hit these constraints mid-refactor when subclass access patterns suddenly break type checking.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript protected vs private in 2026: The Inheritance Visibility Rules That Bite Teams Mid-Refactor

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

The Access Modifier Confusion That Breaks Refactors

Teams discover the difference between protected and private when a seemingly safe refactor suddenly fails type checking. A developer extracts shared logic into a base class, marks a field private, and watches the entire subclass hierarchy reject access to that field. The build breaks. The refactor stalls. The team backtracks to public and ships the leaky abstraction.

The problem: private members vanish the moment inheritance enters the picture. Subclasses cannot touch them. The TypeScript compiler enforces this boundary strictly, treating private as a hard contract between the declaring class and no one else. When developers expect inheritance-friendly visibility, they reach for the wrong modifier and hit a wall mid-refactor.

Problem diagram showing private field blocking subclass access

The solution: protected members expose themselves to the inheritance chain. Subclasses gain access. The refactor proceeds without visibility violations. The type checker passes because the modifier matches the actual access pattern.

Solution diagram showing protected field allowing subclass access

This matters because the wrong choice compounds during maintenance. A private field that should have been protected forces awkward workarounds (public getters, reflection tricks, or abandoning inheritance entirely). Teams that understand the visibility rules ship cleaner hierarchies and avoid the mid-refactor panic when TypeScript refuses to compile.

Key Takeaways

  • private members are invisible to subclasses; only the declaring class can access them, making them unsuitable for inheritance-based patterns.
  • protected members expose themselves to the entire inheritance chain, allowing subclasses to access and override them while still hiding them from external code.
  • TypeScript's structural typing treats private as a nominal constraint: two classes with identically named private fields are incompatible even if their shapes match.
  • Both private and protected disappear during compilation to JavaScript; the runtime offers zero enforcement, making these purely compile-time contracts.
  • Choosing the wrong modifier mid-refactor forces visibility violations that break builds and require either exposing fields as public or redesigning the hierarchy.

How protected and private Actually Work: The Visibility Rules

TypeScript's access modifiers control compile-time visibility, not runtime behavior. The TypeScript handbook defines three visibility levels: public (accessible everywhere, the default), protected (accessible within the class and its subclasses), and private (accessible only within the declaring class). These boundaries exist solely during type checking.

A private member creates a one-class perimeter. The declaring class can read and write it. Subclasses cannot. External code cannot. The TypeScript compiler enforces this by rejecting any access outside the declaring class:

class DatabaseConnection {
  private credentials: string;

  constructor(creds: string) {
    this.credentials = creds; // ✓ allowed in declaring class
  }

  connect() {
    console.log(`Connecting with ${this.credentials}`);
  }
}

class SecureConnection extends DatabaseConnection {
  audit() {
    console.log(this.credentials); // ✗ Property 'credentials' is private
  }
}

The subclass SecureConnection inherits the structure of DatabaseConnection, but the private modifier blocks access. The compiler sees the reference to this.credentials and rejects it. The error message is explicit: Property 'credentials' is private and only accessible within class 'DatabaseConnection'.

A protected member expands the perimeter to include the inheritance chain. The declaring class and all subclasses can access it. External code still cannot. This matches the common pattern where base classes define fields that subclasses need to implement specialized behavior:

class Cache {
  protected storage: Map<string, unknown>;

  constructor() {
    this.storage = new Map(); // ✓ allowed in declaring class
  }

  get(key: string): unknown {
    return this.storage.get(key); // ✓ allowed in declaring class
  }
}

class LRUCache extends Cache {
  private accessOrder: string[] = [];

  get(key: string): unknown {
    const value = this.storage.get(key); // ✓ allowed in subclass
    this.accessOrder.push(key);
    return value;
  }
}

The protected field storage is visible to both Cache and LRUCache. The subclass can directly read the map to implement custom eviction logic. The external API remains unchanged because protected still hides the field from consumers of the class.

TypeScript visibility diagram showing access modifier boundaries

TypeScript does not allow cross-hierarchy protected access. A subclass can access protected members on this, but not on sibling class instances. This prevents a Derived1 instance from reaching into a Derived2 instance's protected state, even though both extend the same base class. The TypeScript handbook explains this as a safeguard against unintended coupling between unrelated subclasses.

The visibility rules create a hierarchy of access: private locks the field to one class, protected extends visibility to descendants, and public removes restrictions entirely. Developers choose based on how the field participates in inheritance.

The Structural Typing Trap: Why private Members Break Type Compatibility

TypeScript uses structural typing for most type checks. Two objects with identical shapes are compatible, regardless of where they were declared. The compiler compares properties, not names or origins. A { x: number } from one file matches a { x: number } from another.

private and protected members break this rule. The TypeScript compiler treats them nominally: two types are compatible only if their private or protected members come from the same declaration. The TypeScript handbook states this explicitly: "For two types to be considered compatible, if one of them has a private member, then the other must have a private member that originated in the same declaration."

This creates surprising incompatibility between structurally identical classes:

class Animal {
  private name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

class Employee {
  private name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

const animal: Animal = new Animal("Dog");
const employee: Employee = new Employee("Alice");

const entity: Animal = employee; // ✗ Type 'Employee' is not assignable to type 'Animal'

Both Animal and Employee have a private name: string field. The shapes are identical. Structural typing would treat them as compatible. The compiler rejects the assignment because the private members originated in different declarations. The name in Animal and the name in Employee are distinct, incompatible types.

Inheritance preserves the declaration origin. A subclass that extends a base class inherits the base's private and protected members, including their declaration origin. This makes the subclass compatible with the base:

class Animal {
  private name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
  constructor(name: string) {
    super(name);
  }
}

const animal: Animal = new Dog("Rex"); // ✓ compatible via inheritance

The private name in Dog originated in Animal. The compiler sees the shared origin and allows the assignment. This nominal check ensures that private members remain truly private: only classes in the same inheritance chain can share them.

This matters during refactors. Extracting a base class with private fields breaks compatibility with any external code that expects the original type. The structural shape remains identical, but the declaration origin changes. Type checks that previously passed now fail.

The workaround: use protected for fields that participate in inheritance, or avoid access modifiers entirely for fields that need structural compatibility.

protected vs private in Inheritance Hierarchies: Real Refactoring Scenarios

Teams hit the protected versus private decision when pulling shared state into a base class. The question: should subclasses access this field directly, or only through methods?

A common scenario: multiple service classes share database connection logic. The initial implementation duplicates the connection field in each class. The refactor extracts a BaseService with the shared connection. The developer marks it private to enforce encapsulation:

class BaseService {
  private connection: DatabaseConnection;

  constructor(conn: DatabaseConnection) {
    this.connection = conn;
  }

  protected query(sql: string): Promise<unknown[]> {
    return this.connection.execute(sql);
  }
}

class UserService extends BaseService {
  async findById(id: number): Promise<User | null> {
    // Must use this.query() instead of direct connection access
    const rows = await this.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`);
    return rows[0] as User;
  }
}

The private connection forces subclasses to use the protected query() method. This works when the base class API covers all use cases. It breaks when a subclass needs direct connection access for transaction management, connection pooling, or custom query building. The refactor stalls. The developer either exposes connection as public (leaking the abstraction) or redesigns the base class API to support every possible use case (overengineering).

The alternative: mark connection as protected. Subclasses gain direct access. The base class still hides it from external code:

class BaseService {
  protected connection: DatabaseConnection;

  constructor(conn: DatabaseConnection) {
    this.connection = conn;
  }
}

class TransactionalUserService extends BaseService {
  async createWithAudit(user: User): Promise<void> {
    const tx = await this.connection.beginTransaction(); // ✓ direct access
    try {
      await tx.execute("INSERT INTO users ...");
      await tx.execute("INSERT INTO audit_log ...");
      await tx.commit();
    } catch (error) {
      await tx.rollback();
      throw error;
    }
  }
}

The subclass uses the connection directly for transaction control. The base class does not need to anticipate every transaction pattern. The protected modifier trusts subclasses to use the connection correctly.

Inheritance hierarchy showing protected field access patterns

Another scenario: a Component base class manages lifecycle state. Subclasses need to read the current state to decide whether to run certain logic. The developer marks state private and adds a getter:

class Component {
  private state: "mounted" | "unmounted" = "unmounted";

  mount() {
    this.state = "mounted";
    this.onMount();
  }

  protected onMount() {
    // hook for subclasses
  }

  isMounted(): boolean {
    return this.state === "mounted";
  }
}

class AsyncComponent extends Component {
  protected onMount() {
    if (this.isMounted()) { // must call getter
      this.loadData();
    }
  }
}

The getter works, but adds indirection. Every subclass that checks state calls isMounted() instead of reading state directly. If the state shape becomes more complex (adding "mounting", "unmounting", "error" states), the base class must add corresponding getters for each state. This scales poorly.

The protected alternative eliminates the getter:

class Component {
  protected state: "mounted" | "unmounted" = "unmounted";

  mount() {
    this.state = "mounted";
    this.onMount();
  }

  protected onMount() {}
}

class AsyncComponent extends Component {
  protected onMount() {
    if (this.state === "mounted") { // direct access
      this.loadData();
    }
  }
}

Subclasses read state directly. The base class does not proliferate getters. The tradeoff: subclasses can mutate state incorrectly. The developer trusts that subclass authors understand the lifecycle contract.

Runtime Reality: Why Both Modifiers Disappear in Compiled JavaScript

TypeScript's access modifiers exist only during type checking. The compiler strips them during transpilation. The emitted JavaScript contains no enforcement, no runtime checks, and no access restrictions. A private field becomes an ordinary property accessible via bracket notation or reflection.

The TypeScript handbook states this explicitly: "Like other aspects of TypeScript's type system, private and protected are only enforced during type checking." The compiled output looks identical for public, protected, and private fields.

class Secure {
  private secret: string;
  protected internal: string;
  public visible: string;

  constructor() {
    this.secret = "hidden";
    this.internal = "shared";
    this.visible = "open";
  }
}

The TypeScript compiler targeting ES2015 emits:

class Secure {
  constructor() {
    this.secret = "hidden";
    this.internal = "shared";
    this.visible = "open";
  }
}

All three fields appear as regular properties. No visibility enforcement. A consumer can access secret and internal directly:

const instance = new Secure();
console.log(instance.secret); // "hidden" — no runtime error
console.log(instance["secret"]); // "hidden" — bracket notation bypasses TypeScript

The TypeScript compiler rejects these accesses during type checking, but the runtime allows them. This creates a disconnect: code that fails to compile still runs successfully if the type checks are bypassed.

JavaScript's #private syntax (standardized in ES2022) provides runtime enforcement. Fields declared with # are truly private: the JavaScript engine prevents external access:

class Secure {
  #secret = "hidden";

  getSecret() {
    return this.#secret; // ✓ internal access allowed
  }
}

const instance = new Secure();
console.log(instance.#secret); // SyntaxError: Private field '#secret' must be declared

The # syntax creates hard privacy. The engine throws an error at runtime, not just during compilation. TypeScript supports this syntax and treats #private fields as truly inaccessible.

Feature TypeScript private TypeScript protected JavaScript #private
Compile-time enforcement Yes (TypeScript only) Yes (TypeScript only) Yes (TypeScript only)
Runtime enforcement No No Yes (JavaScript engine)
Subclass access Blocked Allowed Blocked
External access via bracket notation Allowed at runtime Allowed at runtime Blocked
Transpilation to ES5 Becomes public property Becomes public property Polyfilled with WeakMap

Comparison diagram showing TypeScript private versus JavaScript private fields

Teams that need runtime privacy use #private fields. Teams that need inheritance-friendly visibility use protected. Teams that want compile-time guardrails without runtime overhead stick with TypeScript's private and accept the soft enforcement.

The practical implication: access modifiers are documentation for the type checker and other developers. They communicate intent (this field should not leak outside the class), but they do not prevent malicious or careless access at runtime. Security-critical code requires additional runtime validation.

When to Reach for protected vs private: Decision Framework for 2026

The choice between protected and private depends on whether subclasses need field access. The decision tree starts with one question: will any subclass need to read or write this field directly?

If no subclass needs access, use private. This signals that the field is an implementation detail of the declaring class. Subclasses should not depend on it. Future refactors can change the field's type, name, or behavior without breaking subclasses:

class HttpClient {
  private retryCount: number = 0;
  private maxRetries: number = 3;

  async request(url: string): Promise<Response> {
    while (this.retryCount < this.maxRetries) {
      try {
        return await fetch(url);
      } catch (error) {
        this.retryCount++;
      }
    }
    throw new Error("Max retries exceeded");
  }
}

The retryCount and maxRetries fields manage retry logic internal to HttpClient. No subclass needs to know about them. Marking them private allows the developer to replace the retry mechanism (switching to exponential backoff, for example) without touching subclass code.

If subclasses need access, use protected. This signals that the field participates in the inheritance contract. Subclasses can read and write it to implement specialized behavior:

class Repository {
  protected cache: Map<string, unknown> = new Map();

  get(key: string): unknown | undefined {
    return this.cache.get(key);
  }

  set(key: string, value: unknown): void {
    this.cache.set(key, value);
  }
}

class TTLRepository extends Repository {
  private expirations: Map<string, number> = new Map();

  set(key: string, value: unknown, ttl: number): void {
    this.cache.set(key, value); // ✓ direct cache access
    this.expirations.set(key, Date.now() + ttl);
  }

  get(key: string): unknown | undefined {
    const expiration = this.expirations.get(key);
    if (expiration && Date.now() > expiration) {
      this.cache.delete(key); // ✓ direct cache access
      this.expirations.delete(key);
      return undefined;
    }
    return this.cache.get(key);
  }
}

The protected cache allows TTLRepository to implement expiration logic without duplicating the storage mechanism. The base class trusts subclasses to maintain cache consistency.

Scenario Use private Use protected
Field is pure implementation detail ✓
Subclasses will never need access ✓
Field participates in overridable behavior ✓
Subclasses need direct read/write access ✓
Future subclasses are unknown but likely ✓
Field type may change in future versions ✓

Decision flowchart for choosing between protected and private

A common pattern: use private for fields that drive internal algorithms, and protected for fields that represent shared state. If the field's value affects how subclasses implement their behavior, make it protected. If the field exists only to support the base class's methods, make it private.

The exception: library code intended for public consumption. Public APIs often expose hooks (like React component lifecycle methods) but keep all state private. This prevents consumers from accidentally breaking the library's invariants. The library provides protected methods for subclass customization, but keeps data fields locked.

Migration Patterns: Fixing Mid-Refactor Visibility Violations Without Breaking Everything

Teams discover visibility violations mid-refactor when a subclass suddenly cannot access a field that was previously visible. The fix depends on whether the field should have been protected from the start, or whether the subclass access pattern was a mistake.

The first migration: promoting private to protected. This happens when a developer correctly identified shared state but chose the wrong modifier. The fix is mechanical: change private to protected in the base class. TypeScript recompiles without errors. Subclasses gain access:

// Before: private blocks subclass access
class EventEmitter {
  private listeners: Map<string, Function[]> = new Map();

  on(event: string, handler: Function) {
    const handlers = this.listeners.get(event) || [];
    handlers.push(handler);
    this.listeners.set(event, handlers);
  }
}

class LoggingEmitter extends EventEmitter {
  on(event: string, handler: Function) {
    console.log(`Registering ${event}`);
    // Need to access this.listeners but it's private
  }
}

// After: protected allows subclass access
class EventEmitter {
  protected listeners: Map<string, Function[]> = new Map();

  on(event: string, handler: Function) {
    const handlers = this.listeners.get(event) || [];
    handlers.push(handler);
    this.listeners.set(event, handlers);
  }
}

class LoggingEmitter extends EventEmitter {
  on(event: string, handler: Function) {
    console.log(`Registering ${event}`);
    const handlers = this.listeners.get(event) || []; // ✓ now allowed
    handlers.push(handler);
    this.listeners.set(event, handlers);
    super.on(event, handler);
  }
}

The migration preserves the external API. Code that uses EventEmitter continues working. Only subclass implementations change.

The second migration: demoting protected to private with an accessor layer. This happens when subclass access was a mistake. The base class wants to change the field's implementation without breaking subclasses. The fix: add a protected getter/setter and mark the field private:

// Before: protected exposes implementation detail
class Cache {
  protected storage: Map<string, unknown> = new Map();

  get(key: string): unknown {
    return this.storage.get(key);
  }
}

class MetricsCache extends Cache {
  get(key: string): unknown {
    const value = this.storage.get(key); // direct access
    this.recordHit();
    return value;
  }
}

// After: private field with protected accessor
class Cache {
  private storage: Map<string, unknown> = new Map();

  protected getFromStorage(key: string): unknown {
    return this.storage.get(key);
  }
